messages.subject: Blind strip in aerial surveys
parts:
Dear list,

I am analyzing data collected from a white-tailed deer aerial survey and =
I have=20
a question about how to handle animals observed in the =93blind strip=94 =
(strip=20
directly under the helicopter). Prior to the flights, the bin widths and=
=20
placements were determined by hovering the helicopter at the flight altit=
ude=20
of 60 meters and marking the windows accordingly. It was determined that=
=20
there was a 22 meter strip that was not visible (particularly from the ba=
ck=20
window) and therefore the =930=94 line was offset by 22 meters. The subs=
equent=20
bins were marked in 50 meter intervals. The issue I have with the data i=
s that=20
the observers counted the deer, even if the deer were observed inside tha=
t=20
blind strip. The consensus was that the number of deer that were directl=
y=20
under the helicopter was very few, however, I am still concerned that by=20=

counting the deer in that strip and placing them into the first bin will =
over=20
estimate the density. From reading the archives I believe the solution i=
n the=20
future is allow observers to count all deer, however, have them clearly m=
ark=20
those observations of deer inside the blind strip separate from the 0-50 =
bin.=20=20
That would allow me to left truncate (or simply not include) the under-th=
e-
helicopter-bin in analysis stage. However, this year, the data is alread=
y=20
collected and I have no way of knowing which deer were truly in the=20
first "visible" bin and which were under the helicopter. Also, there wer=
e=20
occasions where deer would move, in response to the approaching helicopte=
r,=20
from under the helicopter to the first strip. Any advice on how to best =
handle=20
this would be appreciated.
Thank you,
Elina=20=20

messages.author: 5140016d70f6ba82
messages.subject: Re: Blind strip in aerial surveys
parts:
Elina-

Your concerns are quite valid. You are in a bit of a pickle. The only=20
thing I can suggest is to bound the results by running the analysis as=20
is with the first bin from 0-50 and a second analysis of 0-72. The=20
first is an upper bound and the second a lower bound.

The solution for next year is what I'd suggest as well. As I state in=20
Ch7 of the Intro DS book (2001), I'm a firm believer in letting the=20
observer "count" all their detections and then handle them as you want=20
in the analysis. Observers want to do a "good" job and to them that=20
often means seeing as much as they can and writing it all down. Often=20
this is a detriment to the result as you found. I've seen many=20
examples. If you set a boundary, sightings outside the boundary "creep"=20
in. I would suggest you do the same thing with the outer bin -- having=20
a category of beyond the last bin. Also, I suggest that you consider=20
having unequal distance bins with increasing bin size with distance --=20
use equal vertical angles. I suggest reading ch7 thoroughly as there=20
maybe other considerations I've not thought of here.

regards --jeff
